readerTitle: Your best friend may not be your best co-founder
caseNote: 가상 사례 두 개 (B2B 컨설팅 회사, 소프트웨어 스타트업) + 실제 연구 (Wasserman의 창업자 연구)
insight: 공동창업자는 편한 사람이 아니라, 기술은 나와 다르고 가치관과 헌신도는 같으며, 이미 함께 일하며 의견 충돌을 넘겨 본 사람이어야 한다.
misconception: 오래 알고 믿는 친구나 나와 비슷한 사람과 시작하는 것이 가장 안전하다.

sources.text: Wasserman, N. (2012). The Founder's Dilemmas: Anticipating and Avoiding the Pitfalls That Can Sink a Startup. Princeton University Press.
두 회사 사례와 모든 세부 내용은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Wasserman이 친구·가족·비슷한 사람과의 공동창업을 '편하지만 위험한(comfortable but dangerous)' 선택으로 설명한 표현을 원문에서 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체 수치 없이 일반적인 결론만 적었습니다.
Wasserman 연구 대상 규모('thousands of founders')는 책 서문 기준으로 확인이 필요합니다. 불확실하면 'many founders'로 바꾸세요.
두 회사(Ledgerline, Shiftwise)는 가상 사례이며 실제 기업명과 겹치지 않는지 게시 전 확인하세요.

cards.title: Your best friend may not be your best co-founder
body: Two small companies launch in the same month. One is a consulting firm started by two close friends. The other is a software startup started by two people who once argued for weeks over a project.
A year later, only one of them is still growing. It isn't the one built on friendship.

image.label: Two founding pairs at separate desks
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 비슷한 옷차림의 두 사람이 똑같은 노트북 앞에서 웃고 있음. 오른쪽은 서로 다른 도구(화이트보드, 노트북)를 든 두 사람이 진지하게 토론 중. 실제 로고나 브랜드 없음.

cards.title: Who do you start with?
body: You're an accountant starting a bookkeeping firm for small businesses. You can do the work well. You've never had to win clients.
Three people are interested in joining as co-founder. Who do you pick?

options.text: Your closest friend, also an accountant, whom you trust completely
options.feedback: You get trust and an easy start. But you'd have two people who can do the work and nobody who brings it in.

options.text: A former colleague who led client sales. You clashed on one project but sorted it out
options.feedback: Different skills cover your gap, and you already know how you both handle a disagreement. The cost is less comfort at the start.

options.text: A sales star you met at an event last month, very keen to start
options.feedback: The skills fit, but you know nothing about how this person behaves under pressure. A month of enthusiasm tells you little about year three.

cards.title: Same start, different second year.
body: **Ledgerline**, the consulting firm, had two friends with the same background. Both loved client work. Neither wanted to sell. Revenue stalled, and each quietly blamed the other for not chasing new clients.

**Shiftwise**, the software startup, paired a developer with an operations manager she'd worked with at a client. They'd fought over scope once and learned how to settle it. One built, one sold. When a hard choice came, they had a way to make it.

cards.title: Different skills, same values, tested together
body: Choosing a co-founder means checking three things. **Skills** should be different, so the team covers more of the business. **Values and commitment** should match: how hard you'll work, how much risk you'll take, how big you want to grow.
And the working relationship should be **tested**. You want to know how this person disagrees before your money and years depend on it.

image.label: Three layers: skills, values, tested relationship
image.brief: 세 개의 층으로 된 인포그래픽. 맨 위 "Skills: different" (서로 다른 모양의 퍼즐 조각이 맞물림), 가운데 "Values & commitment: the same" (같은 방향의 화살표 두 개), 맨 아래 "Relationship: tested" (번개를 지나온 두 선이 다시 이어짐).

cards.title: The comfortable choice is often the risky one.
body: Harvard professor Noam Wasserman studied many startup founding teams for his book *The Founder's Dilemmas*.

He found that founders often pick friends, family or people like themselves because it feels easy. He calls that choice comfortable but dangerous. Similar people tend to share the same blind spots, and close friends often avoid the hard talks about money, roles and effort until it's too late.

cards.title: The questions to ask before you shake hands.
body: This applies to a bakery, a clinic or a design studio as much as to tech. Before committing, talk through:
list: How many hours a week will each of us really give?
How much of our own money can we lose?
Do we want a steady business or a big one?
What happens if one of us wants out?
cards.callout: Different answers here hurt more than different skills ever will.

cards.title: Different can go too far.
body: Complementary skills help only if you can still understand each other. A founder who can't follow the other's work can't judge it or step in when needed.
And not every gap needs a co-founder. If you only need a skill, hiring or paying a freelancer may be cheaper than giving away part of the business for life.

cards.title: Now it's a software app.
body: You're a designer building an app that helps gyms book classes. You need someone technical. Two options look good. Which step comes first?

options.text: Pick the strongest engineer you can find and sign the paperwork fast
options.feedback: You fill the skill gap quickly, but you skip finding out whether your goals and work styles match.

options.text: Run a paid four-week project with each before deciding
options.feedback: It costs time and some money, but you see real disagreements and real effort before anyone owns anything.

options.text: Ask each to describe their values in a long interview
options.feedback: Talking about values is useful. But what people say in an interview is weaker evidence than how they act on a deadline.

cards.title: Pick for different skills, shared values and a tested relationship.
body: Comfort feels safe at the start. What protects the business is a partner who fills your gaps, wants what you want, and has already disagreed with you well.
**Try it today:** write down the skill you lack most and the one thing you'd never compromise on. Check any potential partner against both.
